text: Seldom has medicine advanced as rapidly as it has in the past few decades, yet access to its benefits remains far from equitable. In wealthy nations, an early diagnosis and swift intervention can transform a patient's prognosis, whereas in underfunded regions, the same illness may go untreated until it begins to deteriorate beyond repair. This disparity raises a profound ethical dilemma: how should limited resources be allocated when demand invariably outstrips supply? Were healthcare systems designed purely around efficiency, patient autonomy might be sacrificed for the sake of cost-cutting. Confidentiality, too, is increasingly tested as digital records proliferate, and informed consent grows more complex amid ever more sophisticated treatments. Meanwhile, physicians themselves are not immune to the strain; chronic understaffing has left many on the verge of burnout, undermining the holistic, patient-centered care that reformers advocate. Nowhere are these tensions more visible than in debates over euthanasia and palliative care for the terminally ill, where medical malpractice claims and questions of dignity intersect. Ultimately, building a system that is genuinely accessible to all — not merely to the privileged — will require rehabilitation of both policy and public trust alike.
